title: Humbler than a blade of grass
hookLine: humbler than a blade of grass, more patient than a tree
carry: humbler than grass, you can sing the name always

cards: Step on a blade of grass and it bends flat. Lift your foot and, after a moment, it stands back up. No complaint, no grudge.

A tree stands in the sun all day and gives its shade to whoever sits down, even the one with the axe. Those two humble things, grass and a tree, open a short verse that Chaitanya's tradition treasures.
On the last day with the saints of bhakti, it answers a practical question: how do you keep singing?

teach.b: Chaitanya's followers keep a short set of verses under his name, called the Shikshashtakam, his teaching.
One goes, in plain English: be humbler than a blade of grass, more patient than a tree. Give honor to others, and ask none for yourself. Then you can sing the name of Hari always.
This is how his tradition teaches humility: not as feeling small, but as the condition for staying with God's name. Read it as the fine print under kirtan. Anyone can join the song on the first try.
Staying in it is harder. Pride wants the lead line. Impatience wants the song to end.
Wanting respect turns a chorus into a competition. The verse clears all three away, and what's left can keep singing.
His tradition remembers him living it out in Puri, on the coast, where he spent his later years near the temple of Jagannath.

At the great chariot festival, the Ratha Yatra, he's remembered dancing before the rolling chariot with groups of kirtan singers, lost in the names, the whole crowd caught up with him. Now look back over these four weeks.
Andal and Nammalvar, singing to Vishnu in Tamil. The Nayanars, singing to Shiva. Jnaneshwar, Namdev and Tukaram, walking and singing in Maharashtra.
Kabir and his sharp couplets. Tulsidas and Hanuman's song. Surdas in Yashoda's yard.
Mira, laughing over the cup. And Chaitanya in the street with a drum. Different languages, different names for God.

teach.h: THEY SANG AS IF GOD WERE NEAR.
teach.b: One habit: they sang to God as if God were near.

how: Gaudiya Vaishnavas recite the Shikshashtakam, and the grass-and-tree verse is often sung or quoted before kirtan; at Puri's Ratha Yatra, kirtan groups sing and dance before Jagannath's chariot.

games.q: the chariot of Jagannath is rolling through Puri, crowds on every side, drums everywhere. you're Chaitanya. what do you do?
o: dance and sing in front of the chariot with the kirtan groups.
walk the other way to find some silence.
games.why: his tradition remembers him dancing before the chariot, lost in the names, with the crowd caught up around him.

practice: Many Gaudiya Vaishnavas say this verse before they chant, so try it that way. Say it slowly in your own words: humbler than grass, more patient than a tree, giving honor and asking none.
Let go of one small need to be right or to be noticed. Then say a name of God, Hari, Krishna, or the name you use, a few times, gently.
If you don't pray, say the verse, and bring to mind one person you could honor today without needing anything back.
